description: In Mandarin Pinyin, “a” is usually an open vowel, somewhat like the “a” in “father” or the broad vowel in “spa,” but shorter and more central. In combinations, it can be heard in “ai” (roughly “eye”), “ao” (roughly “ow”), “an” (an open “a” followed by n), and “ang” (a more back, open vowel followed by ng). The exact quality changes slightly depending on the following sound.

thoughts: English speakers may recognize the r-colored quality from American English, but Chinese er is more strongly tied to tongue position and may be a separate syllable or an erhua ending. The distinction between full er and suffix-like -r, along with Chinese tones, requires practice.
description: The Chinese “er” sound is a distinctive r-colored vowel. In a standalone syllable, it can sound like “err,” but Chinese tones change its pitch: for example, 二 is èr and 儿 is ér. At the end of a word, “-r” may be an erhua ending, which adds this r-coloring to the preceding syllable rather than forming a full separate syllable, as in 哪儿 nǎr.

thoughts: Mandarin final o is not exactly the English vowel in “go.” It is generally a short, rounded “aw”-like sound, with a slight w-like onset in 我. English speakers may recognize the general vowel quality but often diphthongize it or pronounce it too much like “oh.”

description: In Mandarin pinyin, “-i” has three main pronunciations. After most consonants, it is a clear “ee” sound, like the vowel in English “machine,” though shorter and purer.
